VIDEO.title: Your Church Can Get Along—and Still Be Divided
VIDEO.series: The Book of Romans, Every Word (playlist of 28 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Romans 15:1-13 · Episode 26 (#26 of 28 in the playlist)
hand: Pursue what only God can produce
SUMMARY: The teacher opens: Christians talk a lot about unity, but churches can tolerate each other and keep the peace without the unity Paul describes in Romans 15. Once you see where biblical unity comes from, you see a deeper spiritual problem behind much division. He reads Romans 15:1-13: the strong bear with the weak and build up their neighbor (15:1-2); Christ did not please Himself (15:3); the Scriptures give perseverance, encouragement and hope (15:4); may God grant you the same mind (15:5-6); accept one another as Christ accepted you (15:7); Christ a servant to the circumcision, that the Gentiles might glorify God (15:8-12); may the God of hope fill you (15:13).

Recap of Romans 1-14: God's covenant faithfulness creates a people through grace, not status; whole-life worship; love that confronts evil and absorbs hostility; submission to authorities; love as the fulfillment of the law, living in the overlap of the ages; and in Romans 14, receive one another rather than divide where God has granted freedom. Romans 15:1-13 concludes everything Paul has built from chapter 12.

Observations: Paul redefines strength (15:1): not freedom to do anything, but the capacity to bear with and build up others. Christ is the pattern (15:3). Scripture is given not only for information but for formation (15:4). Unity is commanded (14:19) yet granted by God (15:5): God's people are commanded to pursue what only He can ultimately produce. The escalation runs from not judging (Romans 14) to sacrificial, Christlike service (Romans 15).

Old Testament background: Psalm 69, David's righteous sufferer, read as a messianic pattern (69:9, also 69:4, 21); the Shema's call to keep God's words on the heart (Deuteronomy 6:6-9); David praising God among the nations (Psalm 18:49; 2 Samuel 22:50); the Song of Moses, quoted from the Septuagint (Deuteronomy 32:43); Psalm 117, the shortest psalm; the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:10). Law, prophets and writings agree: God's endgame is a multiethnic people praising Him together under Messiah.

Why does Paul stack commands (15:1, 2, 7; 14:1, 13, 20) and then pray that God would grant unity (15:5)? The clash in Rome was not only relational but spiritual. People can manufacture tolerance, surface agreement and behavioral compliance, but not a genuine shared mind; that is the Lord's work (John 15; John 17).
The lesson: 'Christians are responsible to pursue unity, but only God has the power to actually produce it.'
QUOTES: Christians are responsible to pursue unity, but only God has the power to actually produce it.
God's people are commanded to pursue what only he can ultimately produce.
Church division isn't just a people problem. It's an abiding problem.
The goal is actually not to pursue unity directly apart from Christ. The goal is just to pursue Christ so that unity follows.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of those without strength and not just please ourselves.
Now may the God of perseverance and encouragement grant you to be of the same mind with one another according to Christ Jesus,
Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you will abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

src.text: Each of us is to please his neighbor for his good, to his building up.

lines.text: Paul reiterates the thrust of Romans 14 (see 14:3, 13, 15-16, 20). Christian strength is shaped by obligation to others: not the freedom to do anything, but the capacity to bear with and build up neighbors so that they mature.
The teacher admits this requires patience and forgiveness in short supply these days, even in himself.

left.text: For zeal for Your house has consumed me, / And the reproaches of those who reproach You have fallen on me.

right.text: For even Christ did not please Himself; but as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached You fell on Me.”

lines.text: Psalm 69, written by David, is taken up in the New Testament as a messianic pattern: 'Those who hate me without cause are more than the hairs of my head' (Psalm 69:4); 'for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink' (Psalm 69:21). Because Jesus bore the reproach of others, we follow His model and bear with the weak.

left.text: These words, which I am commanding you today, shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your sons and shall speak of them when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way and when you lie down and when you rise up.

right.text: For whatever was written in earlier times was written for our instruction, so that through the perseverance and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.

lines.text: The Tanakh, the Old Testament, was written for instruction. Paul's statement fits the scriptural mindset of the Shema. Many Christians have treated Scripture as pure intellectual information rather than what it is intended to be.

left.text: So then let us pursue the things which make for peace and the building up of one another.

right.text: Now may the God of perseverance and encouragement grant you to be of the same mind with one another according to Christ Jesus, so that with one accord you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

lines.text: Is unity a command or something God grants? The answer is both. Paul presses real responsibility on the church (15:1, 2, 7; 14:1, 13, 20), then prays that God would grant harmony.

left.text: Abide in Me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit from itself unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you unless you abide in Me.

right.text: that they may all be one; even as You, Father, are in Me and I in You, that they also may be in Us, so that the world may believe that You sent Me.

lines.text: If abiding in Christ is the condition for bearing fruit, unity is one of those fruits. People can manufacture tolerance, surface agreement and behavioral compliance, but not a genuine shared mind. Pride and tribalism are spiritual indicators that we may be living without truly abiding.

src.text: Therefore, accept one another, just as Christ also accepted us to the glory of God.

lines.text: The escalation runs from not judging brothers and sisters (Romans 14) to serving sacrificially like Christ (Romans 15). The unity Paul is after is not superficial agreement but costly, Christlike love within a divided community.

left.text: Therefore I will give thanks to You among the nations, O Yahweh, / And I will sing praises to Your name. / He gives great salvation to His king, / And shows lovingkindness to His anointed, / To David and his seed forever.

right.text: For I say that Christ has become a servant to the circumcision on behalf of the truth of God to confirm the promises given to the fathers, and for the Gentiles to glorify God for His mercy; as it is written, “Therefore I will give praise to You among the Gentiles, And I will sing to Your name.”

lines.text: Paul quotes Psalm 18:49 (also 2 Samuel 22:50): David praised God in his own context and among the nations, a pattern finding its fullest expression in the Anointed, the Messiah.

left.text: O nations, cause His people to shout for joy; / For He will avenge the blood of His slaves, / And He will render vengeance on His adversaries, / And He will atone for His land and His people.”

right.text: Praise Yahweh, all nations; / Laud Him, all peoples! / For His lovingkindness prevails over us, / And the truth of Yahweh is everlasting. / Praise Yah!

lines.text: In 15:10 Paul cites the Song of Moses from the Septuagint: 'Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people' (Romans 15:10). The Torah itself anticipated Gentile inclusion in Israel's worship, not to replace Israel but to join them.

Psalm 117 is the shortest psalm, and the teacher calls it chiastic. The nations praise God because of His lovingkindness toward Israel: Gentile inclusion was always anticipated in Israel's Scriptures.

left.text: Then it will be in that day, / That the nations will seek the root of Jesse, / Who will stand as a standard for the peoples; / And His resting place will be glorious.

right.text: And again Isaiah says, / “There shall come the root of Jesse, / And He who arises to rule over the Gentiles, / In Him shall the Gentiles hope.”

lines.text: Isaiah 11:1-10 is an eschatological promise of the righteous shoot of Jesse. Paul quotes the Septuagint, so his version reads 'hope'. He draws from the Law, the Prophets and the Writings to show that all agree: God's endgame is a multiethnic people praising Him together under Messiah.

BACKGROUND.p: Jewish tradition divides the Scriptures into three parts. Paul's chain in 15:9-12 draws on all three: the Writings (Psalms 18 and 117), the Law (Deuteronomy 32) and the Prophets (Isaiah 11).

Paul often quotes the Septuagint, the Greek translation used in synagogues across the Mediterranean. Its wording of Deuteronomy 32:43 and Isaiah 11:10 differs from the Hebrew text the LSB translates, which is why the Old Testament verses here read differently from Paul's quotations.

BACKGROUND.h: Strong and weak in a status-minded city
BACKGROUND.p: Roman society prized status and the strong expected deference. Paul turns that upside down: the strong are obligated to the weak, after the pattern of Christ (15:1-3).

DEBATES.p: Paul counts himself among them ('we who are strong'). Many read the strong as mostly Gentile-background believers, with some Jewish believers like Paul; the weak as those, often Jewish-background, who kept food laws and days.

The Hebrew text, followed by the LSB, reads 'O nations, cause His people to shout for joy'; the Septuagint, which Paul quotes, reads 'Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people'. Scholars discuss whether Paul chose the Greek wording for its fit with his argument or simply used the Bible his readers knew.
Some read it as Christ's ministry among Jews; others as His serving God's covenant with Israel, confirming the promises to the fathers so that Gentiles also might glorify God.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says Paul prays 'once in Romans 15:3 and again in verse 13.' Romans 15:3 is the quotation of Psalm 69:9; the first prayer is 15:5-6.
The captions render several ranges oddly, such as 'verses 8-2', 'verses 9-2' and 'chapters 12-4'; the sense is 15:8-12, 15:9-12 and chapters 12-14.

QUESTIONS: How does Paul's definition of strength in 15:1 differ from how you usually think of strength?
Where are you reading Scripture for information but not for formation?
Why would Paul command unity and then pray for God to grant it?
What does Psalm 117 teach about why the nations praise God?
What would it look like this week to pursue Christ so that unity follows?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: Church division isn't just a people problem; it's an abiding problem. Where abiding is absent, division becomes inevitable over time, no matter how strong the theology or structure. The teacher confesses that abiding is something he needs to improve: a perpetual returning to solitude, rest and God's quiet presence. A pastor friend told him it takes as much work to rest as to work. When he does not abide, he has less patience, grace and mercy for difficult people. As he has leaned into abiding, his early, more aggressive videos have given way to a softer heart, even toward aggressive critics, remembering he was once like them and that they bear God's image. 'The church is the only army that shoots its own wounded,' the opposite of Spirit-produced unity. The action step is counterintuitive: not to pursue unity directly apart from Christ, but to pursue Christ so that unity follows.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): set aside ten quiet minutes each day this week with John 15:1-11. At the end of the week, write down one relationship in your church where you notice your patience has changed.

## Key people

## Places [Background]
- Rome (named in the video): Strong and weak, Jewish- and Gentile-background believers, called to one voice.
- Corinth: Where Paul probably wrote Romans.
- Jerusalem: Zion, from which the root of Jesse would rule (Isaiah 11).

## Key terms
- The strong and the weak: Believers with greater freedom of conscience, and those with more scruples (14:1; 15:1).
- Building up: Helping another believer mature spiritually (15:2).
- Septuagint: The Greek Old Testament, which Paul quotes in 15:10 and 15:12.
- Tanakh: The Hebrew Bible: Law, Prophets and Writings.
- Chiasm: A mirrored literary structure; the video says Psalm 117 is chiastic.
- Abiding: Remaining in Christ as a branch in the vine (John 15:4-5); in the video, the source of unity.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Law, Prophets and Writings: Jewish tradition divides the Scriptures into three parts. Paul's chain in 15:9-12 draws on all three: the Writings (Psalms 18 and 117), the Law (Deuteronomy 32) and the Prophets (Isaiah 11).
- Quoting the Greek Old Testament: Paul often quotes the Septuagint, the Greek translation used in synagogues across the Mediterranean. Its wording of Deuteronomy 32:43 and Isaiah 11:10 differs from the Hebrew text the LSB translates, which is why the Old Testament verses here read differently from Paul's quotations.
- Strong and weak in a status-minded city: Roman society prized status and the strong expected deference. Paul turns that upside down: the strong are obligated to the weak, after the pattern of Christ (15:1-3).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Who are the strong? (15:1) Paul counts himself among them ('we who are strong'). Many read the strong as mostly Gentile-background believers, with some Jewish believers like Paul; the weak as those, often Jewish-background, who kept food laws and days.
- Paul's text of Deuteronomy 32:43 (15:10) The Hebrew text, followed by the LSB, reads 'O nations, cause His people to shout for joy'; the Septuagint, which Paul quotes, reads 'Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people'. Scholars discuss whether Paul chose the Greek wording for its fit with his argument or simply used the Bible his readers knew.
- Christ a servant 'to the circumcision' (15:8) Some read it as Christ's ministry among Jews; others as His serving God's covenant with Israel, confirming the promises to the fathers so that Gentiles also might glorify God.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says Paul prays 'once in Romans 15:3 and again in verse 13.' Romans 15:3 is the quotation of Psalm 69:9; the first prayer is 15:5-6.
- The captions render several ranges oddly, such as 'verses 8-2', 'verses 9-2' and 'chapters 12-4'; the sense is 15:8-12, 15:9-12 and chapters 12-14.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. How does Paul's definition of strength in 15:1 differ from how you usually think of strength?
2. Where are you reading Scripture for information but not for formation?
3. Why would Paul command unity and then pray for God to grant it?
4. What does Psalm 117 teach about why the nations praise God?
5. What would it look like this week to pursue Christ so that unity follows?

## Application
- (video) Church division isn't just a people problem; it's an abiding problem. Where abiding is absent, division becomes inevitable over time, no matter how strong the theology or structure. The teacher confesses that abiding is something he needs to improve: a perpetual returning to solitude, rest and God's quiet presence. A pastor friend told him it takes as much work to rest as to work. When he does not abide, he has less patience, grace and mercy for difficult people. As he has leaned into abiding, his early, more aggressive videos have given way to a softer heart, even toward aggressive critics, remembering he was once like them and that they bear God's image. 'The church is the only army that shoots its own wounded,' the opposite of Spirit-produced unity. The action step is counterintuitive: not to pursue unity directly apart from Christ, but to pursue Christ so that unity follows.
- Study note (added): set aside ten quiet minutes each day this week with John 15:1-11. At the end of the week, write down one relationship in your church where you notice your patience has changed.
